task.request: The dashboard feels slow. Use popup to explore what to improve and the tradeoffs with me.
task.context: A trace already shows a 900 ms server response, including 620 ms spent in repeated per-account database queries. The browser then spends 350 ms rendering a 2,000-row table. Billing data must be fresh immediately after an edit; summary reporting may lag by 30 seconds. Search must still cover all rows. We have no query plan yet. There is no approval to add infrastructure. The team can change the SQL and frontend.
task.combined_intent: Explore batching the repeated queries and reducing rendered rows together; keep search across the full data set and fresh billing edits.
task.correction: Do the query-plan investigation first. We learned that keyboard users rely on the full table, so don't implement virtualization yet.

elements.markdown: The trace gives us two concrete targets: repeated per-account queries consume 620 ms of the 900 ms server response, and rendering the 2,000-row table takes another 350 ms. Query work is the larger measured opportunity, but eliminating all 620 ms is not a realistic promise. We still need a query plan to distinguish repeated round trips from expensive scans or joins. The remaining server work also needs to stay visible in measurements.

I propose investigating a batched SQL read and a smaller rendered table together. They address separate costs and fit the team's ability to change SQL and frontend. Billing must remain fresh immediately after edits, and search must cover the entire data set even when fewer rows are displayed. A 30-second reporting cache is a separate possibility only for summaries; no new infrastructure is assumed.

Review the findings first.markdown: The investigation should return the dominant cost, a concrete SQL proposal, and its correctness risks. If repeated round trips dominate, batching is a strong candidate; if scans or join expansion dominate, the plan may point elsewhere. We cannot select an index or predict a speedup from this trace alone.

Try a local batching prototype.default: Compare results against the existing query path across representative accounts and filters. After a billing edit, refetch authoritative billing data and verify the updated value appears immediately; do not route billing reads through a stale summary cache. Measure query count, database time and total server response on the same workload.

options.value: Keep the full table and profile rendering
options.description: Preserve full-table interaction while checking expensive cells and unnecessary rerenders; savings are uncertain.

Pagination.default: Start with a prototype displaying 50 matching rows per page. Search and sort across all rows before slicing a page, show total matches, and reset to the first page when the search changes. Preserve table headers, keyboard navigation and focus after paging or editing; refresh edited billing values immediately.

Pagination.markdown: Searching only the displayed page would violate your requirement. We need to inspect whether search currently runs over all loaded rows or on the server before choosing where pagination belongs. The proposed page size is a benchmark starting point, not an established optimum.

Virtualization.markdown: Virtualization removes off-screen rows from the rendered table. Search must still run over the full data set. Before implementing it, inspect keyboard and assistive-technology workflows, including finding and focusing an off-screen result; browser find may no longer cover every row. If users depend on the complete rendered table, preserve that workflow and investigate another rendering change.

Virtualization.default: Inspect existing keyboard navigation, screen-reader semantics, browser-find expectations and row-edit behavior. Prototype only after those requirements are understood, with full-data search and explicit focus handling for off-screen results.

Keep the full table and profile renderin.default: Profile initial rendering and a billing edit with all 2,000 rows present. Identify expensive cells, layout work and rows rerendered unnecessarily. Propose targeted changes that preserve search, table semantics, navigation and immediate billing updates.

Allow brief summary staleness.markdown: A 30-second allowance creates room to reuse summary results, but it does not prove caching will reduce this request's cost. First identify which query work belongs to summaries and whether existing application facilities can reuse those results. Billing edit responses and authoritative billing reads must remain fresh. Infrastructure additions require a separate decision.

Allow brief summary staleness.default: Investigate reuse only for summary reporting, with a maximum age of 30 seconds. Keep billing edit results and billing reads authoritative and fresh. Verify permissions and tenant boundaries in any reuse key, and use existing application facilities only. If safe reuse is unavailable, report that constraint before proposing infrastructure.

reveals.markdown: These defaults are editable proposals. The next step should establish missing evidence before committing to an implementation: query plans for SQL, current search and navigation behavior for the table, and a clear reporting boundary for any stale summaries.

elements.markdown: With batching and table work selected, measure each separately and then together on the same representative account set and search. Record database time, total server response and browser rendering time independently so one improvement does not conceal a regression in the other. In every comparison, verify full-data search and immediate billing updates.
elements.when: selected(improvements, Batch the account queries) && selected(improvements, Render fewer table rows)

elements.markdown: The trace identifies two separate costs: **900 ms on the server**, including **620 ms in repeated per-account queries**, followed by **350 ms rendering 2,000 rows**. I would investigate batching first and explore rendering improvements alongside it. The timings identify useful targets, but do not establish the savings: we have no query plan, and a combined query could still scan or join too much data. SQL and frontend changes are available; adding infrastructure is outside the current scope.

options.description: Targets the measured 620 ms; inspect plans and preserve account boundaries and billing correctness before rewriting SQL.
Targets the measured 350 ms; pagination or virtualization must preserve search across all rows and usable navigation.

Batch the account queries.markdown: Batching is a hypothesis, not yet a proven fix. Inspect the repeated query shape, query count, parameters and execution plans on a representative workload. Compare a set-based or bulk-fetch alternative, checking row counts and per-account results; reducing round trips can help while a large join can introduce duplication or extra work.

Investigate plans first.default: Capture the repeated SQL and its query count; inspect execution plans using an appropriate safe environment; identify whether round trips, scans or joins dominate; return a batching proposal with correctness risks and a benchmark design. Stop before implementation if representative data or safe execution is unavailable.

Investigate and benchmark a prototype.default: After inspecting plans, prototype one batched SQL path in a test environment. Compare identical account sets, result values, query count and response timings with the baseline. Preserve account access boundaries and immediate post-edit billing reads. Report findings before adopting the rewrite.

Render fewer table rows.markdown: Fewer mounted rows should reduce browser work, but changing what is displayed must not narrow what can be searched. Pagination is explicit and easier to reason about; virtualization keeps scrolling continuous but needs careful keyboard, focus and assistive-technology handling. We have not established how users navigate the full table.

Inspect usage before changing the table.default: Profile which table work accounts for the 350 ms and inspect search, sorting, keyboard navigation and accessibility behavior. Allow summary reporting to lag.markdown: A separate summary freshness policy could avoid repeated computation, but we do not know how much summary work contributes to this trace. First inspect the existing data path and any existing cache. A 30-second allowance is a maximum age, not permission to return stale billing data after an edit or to add a new service.

Allow summary reporting to lag.default: Investigate whether summaries can reuse results for at most 30 seconds using the existing application architecture. Keep billing reads separate and fresh immediately after edits. Check account scoping and stale-result behavior. If the approach requires new infrastructure or contributes little measured savings, report that before proceeding.

elements.markdown: With SQL and rendering work selected, measure each separately before combining them. Use the same account set and 2,000-row workload to compare server response time, repeated-query time and browser rendering. Include a search for an initially undisplayed row and an immediate read after a billing edit. This distinguishes faster SQL from fewer mounted rows and catches a fast result that is stale or incomplete.
